p.src: The great affairs of the realm follow a general course: after long division comes unity, and after long unity comes division. At the end of the Zhou dynasty, seven states contended until they were united under Qin. After Qin fell, Chu and Han fought for mastery, and the realm was united once more under Han. The Han dynasty began when Gaozu slew the White Serpent and raised the banner of revolt, and he brought all the realm under one rule. Later, Emperor Guangwu restored the dynasty; but when the succession reached Emperor Xian, the realm at last divided into three kingdoms. Tracing the causes of the disorder, they seem to have begun in the reigns of Emperors Huan and Ling. Emperor Huan proscribed the worthy and placed his trust in the eunuchs. When Emperor Huan died and Emperor Ling ascended the throne, General-in-Chief Dou Wu and Grand Tutor Chen Fan together assisted the young sovereign. At the time, the eunuch Cao Jie and his fellows were abusing their power. Dou Wu and Chen Fan plotted to execute them, but their preparations were not kept secret; instead, they themselves were killed, and from then on the palace eunuchs grew ever more overbearing.

p.src: On the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the second year of Jianning, the Emperor held court in the Hall of Warm Virtue. Just as he was mounting the throne, a violent wind suddenly rose at a corner of the hall. A huge green serpent flew down from a roof beam and coiled itself upon the imperial seat. The Emperor collapsed in fright. His attendants hurriedly carried him into the inner palace, while all the officials fled for safety. A moment later, the serpent vanished. Suddenly thunder roared and rain poured down, mingled with hail. The storm did not cease until midnight and destroyed countless houses. In the second month of the fourth year of Jianning, an earthquake struck Luoyang; the sea also flooded, and great waves swept all the coastal inhabitants into the waters. In the first year of Guanghe, a hen changed into a cock. On the first day of the sixth month, a mass of black vapor more than a hundred feet long flew into the Hall of Warm Virtue. In the seventh month of that autumn, a rainbow appeared in the Jade Hall, and the cliffs of the Wuyuan mountains all split and collapsed. These were but some among many ominous portents. The Emperor issued an edict asking his ministers the cause of these calamities and portents. Cai Yong, an advisory gentleman, submitted a memorial arguing that the fallen rainbow and the transformed fowl had been caused by women and eunuchs interfering in government; his words were notably forthright and severe. After reading the memorial, the Emperor sighed, then rose to change his robes. Cao Jie secretly read it from behind, revealed its contents to his associates, and later framed Cai Yong on another charge, causing him to be banished to his native village. Later, Zhang Rang, Zhao Zhong, Feng Xu, Duan Gui, Cao Jie, Hou Lan, Jian Shuo, Cheng Kuang, Xia Yun, and Guo Sheng formed a corrupt faction. These ten were known as the “Ten Regular Attendants.” The Emperor revered and trusted Zhang Rang, calling him his “foster father.” The government worsened by the day, until the people throughout the realm longed for upheaval and bandits rose everywhere like swarming bees.

p.src: At that time, three brothers lived in Julu Commandery: the first was named Zhang Jue, the second Zhang Bao, and the third Zhang Liang. Zhang Jue had once been an unsuccessful scholar. One day, while gathering medicinal herbs in the mountains, he met an old man with emerald eyes and a youthful face, holding a staff of goosefoot wood. The old man summoned Jue into a cave and gave him three volumes of a heavenly book, saying, “This work is called The Essential Arts of Great Peace. Having received it, you must proclaim Heaven’s transforming way and bring salvation to all people. But if you harbor any disloyal intent, you will surely meet with terrible retribution.” Jue bowed and asked the old man’s name. The old man replied, “I am the Old Immortal of the Southern Land.” As soon as he had spoken, he changed into a breath of pure wind and vanished. After obtaining the book, Jue studied and practiced its arts day and night. He learned to summon wind and call down rain, and styled himself the “Adept of Great Peace.” In the first month of the first year of Zhongping, an epidemic spread through the land. Zhang Jue distributed talismanic water and used it to treat the sick, calling himself the “Great and Worthy Master.” Jue had more than five hundred disciples who wandered throughout the realm, and all of them could draw talismans and recite incantations. Thereafter his followers multiplied by the day. Jue organized them into thirty-six divisions: the larger had more than ten thousand members, and the smaller six or seven thousand. Over each he appointed a leader bearing the title of general. He spread the saying, “The Blue Heaven is dead; the Yellow Heaven shall rise. In the year jiazi, great fortune shall come to all beneath Heaven.” He ordered everyone to write the two characters “jiazi” in white clay upon the main gate of the household. Throughout the eight provinces of Qing, You, Xu, Ji, Jing, Yang, Yan, and Yu, every household revered the name of Zhang Jue, the Great and Worthy Master. Jue sent his partisan Ma Yuanyi in secret with gifts of gold and silk to win over the palace eunuch Feng Xu as an ally within the court. Jue conferred with his two younger brothers, saying, “Nothing is harder to win than the hearts of the people. Now that the people’s hearts have turned to us, it would truly be a pity not to seize the moment and take the realm.” So on the one hand he secretly made yellow banners and fixed a date for the uprising; on the other, he sent his disciple Tang Zhou with a letter to inform Feng Xu. Tang Zhou instead went straight to the government offices and revealed the plot. The Emperor summoned General-in-Chief He Jin and ordered him to muster troops, seize Ma Yuanyi, and behead him; then Feng Xu and all his associates were arrested and cast into prison. When Zhang Jue learned that the plot had been exposed, he raised his forces that very night. He styled himself the “General-Lord of Heaven,” Zhang Bao the “General-Lord of Earth,” and Zhang Liang the “General-Lord of Men”; and he proclaimed to the multitude, “The destiny of Han is nearing its end, and a great sage has appeared. All of you should obey Heaven and follow the righteous way, that you may rejoice in an age of great peace.” From every quarter, four or five hundred thousand common people wrapped yellow scarves around their heads and joined Zhang Jue’s rebellion. The rebels’ power was immense, and the imperial troops crumbled at the mere sight of them. He Jin petitioned the Emperor to issue an urgent edict commanding every district to prepare its defenses and earn merit by suppressing the rebels; at the same time, he dispatched the Gentlemen Generals of the Household Lu Zhi, Huangfu Song, and Zhu Jun, each at the head of elite troops, to attack along three separate routes.

p.src: Now Zhang Jue’s army advanced upon the borders of You Province. Liu Yan, the governor of You Province, was a native of Jingling in Jiangxia and a descendant of Prince Gong of Lu of the Han dynasty. On hearing that the rebel army was approaching, he summoned Commandant Zou Jing to discuss their response. Zou Jing said, “The rebels are many and our troops are few. My lord, you should recruit soldiers at once to meet the enemy.” Liu Yan approved his advice and immediately posted notices calling for volunteer troops. When the notice reached Zhuo County, it brought forth a hero who lived there. This man cared little for book learning; he was generous and mild in nature, spoke little, and did not show joy or anger upon his face; he had always cherished lofty ambitions and delighted above all in befriending the heroes of the realm; he stood seven feet five inches tall, with earlobes reaching his shoulders and arms so long that his hands hung below his knees. His eyes could look back upon his own ears; his face was as fair as crowned jade, and his lips as red as if painted with rouge; he was a descendant of Liu Sheng, Prince Jing of Zhongshan, and a distant great-grandson of Emperor Jing of Han. His family name was Liu, his given name Bei, and his courtesy name Xuande. Long before, Liu Sheng’s son Liu Zhen had been enfeoffed as Marquis of Zhuolu Village under Emperor Wu of Han. Later he lost his title for failing to contribute the proper ceremonial gold, and this branch of the family was consequently left in Zhuo County. Xuande’s grandfather was Liu Xiong, and his father Liu Hong. Liu Hong had been nominated as Filial and Incorrupt and had also served as an official, but he died young. Xuande lost his father while still a child and served his mother with the utmost devotion; his family was poor, and he earned his living by selling sandals and weaving mats. His home was in Lousang Village in that county. Southeast of his house stood a great mulberry tree more than fifty feet tall. Seen from afar, its luxuriant crown resembled the canopy of a carriage. A physiognomist once said, “A man of great rank will surely arise from this household.” When Xuande was young, he played beneath the tree with the village children and said, “When I become the Son of Heaven, I shall ride beneath a canopy like this.” His uncle Liu Yuanqi marveled at these words and said, “This child is no ordinary person!” Seeing that Xuande’s family was poor, he thereafter regularly provided for them. At the age of fifteen, Xuande was sent away by his mother to pursue his studies. He studied under Zheng Xuan and Lu Zhi and became friends with Gongsun Zan and others. By the time Liu Yan posted his notices recruiting soldiers, Xuande was already twenty-eight years old.

p.src: That day, when he saw the proclamation, he heaved a sorrowful sigh. A man behind him cried sternly, “Why does a true man sigh instead of serving his country?” Xuande turned and looked at him: he stood eight feet tall, with a panther’s head, great round eyes, a swallow’s jaw, and a tiger’s whiskers; his voice was like mighty thunder, and his bearing like a galloping horse. Seeing his extraordinary appearance, Xuande asked his name. The man said, “My family name is Zhang, my given name Fei, and my courtesy name Yide. My family has long lived in Zhuo Commandery. I own some fields and an estate, and make my living selling wine and slaughtering pigs, but above all I delight in befriending the heroes of the realm. Just now I saw you sigh as you read the proclamation, and so I asked.” Xuande said, “I am a kinsman of the Han imperial house. My family name is Liu and my given name Bei. Now I hear that the Yellow Turbans have raised a rebellion, and I aspire to destroy the rebels and bring peace to the people; but I bitterly regret that I lack the power, and that is why I sighed.” Fei said, “I possess a fair amount of wealth. Let us recruit brave men from the countryside and undertake this great cause together. What say you?” Xuande was overjoyed, and the two went into a village tavern to drink. While they were drinking, they saw a burly man pushing a cart; he stopped at the tavern door, entered, sat down, and called to the server, “Bring me wine quickly! I must hurry into the city to enlist.” Xuande observed the man: he stood nine feet tall, with a beard two feet long; his face was the hue of a ripe jujube, and his lips seemed painted with rouge; he had phoenix eyes and silkworm brows, a majestic countenance and an awe-inspiring bearing. Xuande invited him to share their table and asked his name. The man said, “My family name is Guan, my given name Yu, and my courtesy name was Changsheng, though I later changed it to Yunchang. I am from Xieliang in Hedong. A powerful local bully relied on his influence to oppress others, so I killed him; I have wandered in exile for five or six years. Now I have heard that troops are being raised here to destroy the rebels, so I came expressly to enlist.” Xuande then told him of his own ambitions. Yunchang was delighted. Together they went to Zhang Fei’s estate to discuss their great undertaking.

p.src: Fei said, “Behind my estate is a peach garden where the blossoms are now at their finest. Tomorrow, let us offer sacrifices to Heaven and Earth there and become sworn brothers. Then, united in heart and strength, we may pursue our great cause.” Xuande and Yunchang answered together, “An excellent proposal.” The next day, in the peach garden, they prepared a black ox, a white horse, and other sacrificial offerings. The three burned incense, bowed twice, and swore: “We, Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei, though born to different families, have now become brothers; henceforth we shall unite our hearts and strength, rescue those in distress, and aid those in peril. Above, we shall repay the country; below, we shall bring peace to the common people. We ask not to have been born in the same year, the same month, and the same day; we ask only to die in the same year, the same month, and the same day. May sovereign Heaven and sustaining Earth bear true witness to our hearts. Should any of us betray righteousness and forget this bond, may Heaven and man alike strike him down!” When the oath was complete, they acknowledged Xuande as eldest brother, Guan Yu as second, and Zhang Fei as youngest. After sacrificing to Heaven and Earth, they slaughtered another ox, laid out wine, and gathered more than three hundred brave men from the countryside, all of whom drank their fill in the peach garden. The next day they began preparing weapons, but regretted that they had no horses to ride. As they were pondering this, someone reported that two guests were approaching the estate with a company of attendants and a herd of horses. Xuande said, “This is Heaven’s aid!” The three went out of the estate to welcome them. The two visitors proved to be great merchants from Zhongshan: one was named Zhang Shiping and the other Su Shuang. Every year they traveled north to trade in horses, but had lately turned back because bandits had arisen. Xuande invited them into the estate, entertained them with wine, and explained his intention to destroy the rebels and bring peace to the people. The two merchants were delighted and offered them fifty fine horses; they also presented five hundred taels of gold and silver and a thousand catties of fine iron, to supply their equipment. After thanking the two guests and bidding them farewell, Xuande ordered skilled smiths to forge him a pair of double-edged swords. Yunchang had the Green Dragon Crescent Blade made, also called the “Cold Beauty Saw,” weighing eighty-two catties. Zhang Fei had an eighteen-foot, steel-tipped serpent spear made. Each also acquired a full suit of armor. Having assembled more than five hundred local volunteers, they went to see Zou Jing. Zou Jing presented them to the governor, Liu Yan. After the three had paid their respects, each gave his name. When Xuande recounted his lineage, Liu Yan was delighted and acknowledged him as his nephew.

p.src: Within a few days, word came that the Yellow Turban general Cheng Yuanzhi was leading fifty thousand troops against Zhuo Commandery. Liu Yan ordered Zou Jing to lead Xuande and his two companions, with five hundred troops, to meet and destroy the enemy. Xuande and his companions gladly led their force forward until they reached the foot of Daxing Mountain, where they encountered the rebels. The rebels all wore their hair loose, with yellow cloths bound around their brows. The two armies drew up opposite each other. Xuande rode forward, Yunchang on his left and Yide on his right, raised his whip, and shouted abuse: “Traitorous rebels against the realm, why do you not surrender at once?” Enraged, Cheng Yuanzhi sent his deputy Deng Mao out to fight. Zhang Fei leveled his eighteen-foot serpent spear and charged straight out. With a single thrust he pierced Deng Mao through the heart, pitching him backward from his horse. Seeing Deng Mao slain, Cheng Yuanzhi spurred his horse, brandished his blade, and charged straight at Zhang Fei. Yunchang swung his great blade and galloped out to meet him. Enraged, Cheng Yuanzhi sent his deputy Deng Mao out to fight.
Zhang Fei leveled his eighteen-foot serpent spear and charged straight out. With a single thrust he pierced Deng Mao through the heart, pitching him backward from his horse.
Seeing Deng Mao slain, Cheng Yuanzhi spurred his horse, brandished his blade, and charged straight at Zhang Fei.
Yunchang swung his great blade and galloped out to meet him.
At the sight of him, Cheng Yuanzhi was startled and, before he could defend himself, Yunchang’s rising blade cut him in two.

p.src: When the rebels saw Cheng Yuanzhi slain, they all cast down their weapons and fled. Xuande waved his army forward in pursuit. Countless rebels surrendered, and he returned in great victory. Liu Yan came out in person to welcome them and rewarded the soldiers for their service. The next day, a dispatch arrived from Gong Jing, governor of Qingzhou, stating that Yellow Turban rebels had surrounded the city, which was on the verge of falling, and pleading for aid. Liu Yan discussed the matter with Xuande. Xuande said, “I am willing to go to their rescue.” Liu Yan ordered Zou Jing to take five thousand troops and march to Qingzhou with Xuande, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei. When the rebels saw the relief force arrive, they divided their troops and plunged into a confused battle. Outnumbered, Xuande’s force could not prevail and withdrew thirty li to make camp. Xuande said to Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, “The enemy is numerous and we are few; only an unexpected stratagem can bring us victory.” He therefore assigned Lord Guan a thousand men to lie in ambush to the left of the hills, and Zhang Fei another thousand to lie in ambush to the right. At the signal of the gong, both were to charge out in support. The next day, Xuande and Zou Jing led their troops forward with drums beating and shouts resounding. The rebels came out to meet them, whereupon Xuande led his troops in retreat. The rebels pressed their advantage and pursued. Just as they crossed the ridge, Xuande’s army sounded the gongs together; the two flanking forces charged out, and Xuande wheeled his troops around to renew the attack. Attacked from three directions, the rebels collapsed in rout. They pursued the rebels all the way to the walls of Qingzhou, where Governor Gong Jing also led the militia out of the city to join the battle. The rebels suffered a crushing defeat and were slaughtered in great numbers; thus the siege of Qingzhou was lifted. A later poet praised Xuande in these words:

p.src: After Gong Jing had rewarded the troops, Zou Jing wished to return. Xuande said, “I recently heard that General of the Household Lu Zhi is fighting the rebel leader Zhang Jue at Guangzong. I once studied under Lu Zhi and wish to go to his aid.” Thus Zou Jing led his own army back, while Xuande, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei took their five hundred men toward Guangzong. On reaching Lu Zhi’s army, they entered his tent, paid their respects, and fully explained why they had come. Lu Zhi was delighted and kept them before his tent to await orders.

p.src: At that time Zhang Jue’s rebel host numbered one hundred and fifty thousand, while Lu Zhi had fifty thousand troops. The two armies faced each other at Guangzong, with victory yet undecided. Lu Zhi said to Xuande, “I am holding the rebels in check here. The rebel leader’s brothers, Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao, are at Yingchuan, confronting Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun. Take your own men, and I shall reinforce you with a thousand imperial troops. Go to Yingchuan, learn the situation there, and arrange a date for a concerted attack.” Xuande accepted the order and led his troops toward Yingchuan, marching day and night. At that time Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun were leading their armies against the rebels. After suffering reverses in battle, the rebels withdrew into Changshe and made camp amid the grasslands. Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun conferred: “The rebels have camped amid dry grass. We should attack them with fire.” They therefore ordered every soldier to bind a bundle of grass and lie hidden in ambush. That night, a strong wind suddenly arose. After the second watch, they set the fires all at once, while Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun each led troops against the rebel camp. Flames towered to the sky; the rebels panicked, with no time to saddle their horses or don their armor, and scattered in every direction.

p.src: The fighting raged until dawn, when Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao led their defeated remnants in a desperate flight. Suddenly, a body of troops appeared before them, all bearing red banners, and blocked their way. From their head rode forth a commander, seven feet tall, with narrow eyes and a long beard. He held the office of Commandant of Cavalry. A native of Qiao County in the state of Pei, his surname was Cao, his given name Cao, and his courtesy name Mengde. Cao Cao's father, Cao Song, had originally borne the surname Xiahou. But because he became the adopted son of Cao Teng, a Regular Palace Attendant, he assumed the surname Cao. Cao Song fathered Cao Cao, whose childhood name was A-Man and who was also called Jili. In his youth, Cao Cao loved hunting and roaming abroad, and delighted in song and dance. He was resourceful, calculating, and endlessly adaptable. Cao Cao had an uncle who, seeing the young man indulge himself without restraint, often rebuked him and reported his conduct to Cao Song. Cao Song would then reprimand his son. Then Cao Cao devised a scheme: when he saw his uncle approaching, he fell to the ground and pretended to suffer a seizure. Alarmed, the uncle told Cao Song, who hurried over to see him; but Cao Cao was perfectly well. Cao Song said, “Your uncle told me you had suffered a seizure. Have you recovered already?” Cao Cao replied, “Your son has never suffered from such an illness. I have merely lost my uncle's affection, and so he has deceived you about me.” Cao Song believed him. Thereafter, whenever the uncle reported Cao Cao's misdeeds, Cao Song paid no heed. Thus Cao Cao was free to indulge himself as he pleased. A man of the time named Qiao Xuan once said to Cao Cao, “The realm is about to fall into disorder, and none but an extraordinary genius can save it. Might you be the one who will restore peace?” When He Yong of Nanyang met Cao Cao, he declared, “The house of Han is about to perish; the man who brings peace to the realm will surely be this one.” Xu Shao of Runan was famed as a judge of character. Cao Cao went to see him and asked, “What manner of man am I?” Xu Shao made no reply. Cao Cao asked again, and Xu Shao said, “In times of peace, you would be an able minister; in times of chaos, a treacherous hero.” Cao Cao was delighted to hear this. At twenty, he was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt, appointed a Gentleman, and then made Northern Commandant of Luoyang. As soon as he assumed office, he set up more than ten cudgels painted in five colors at the four gates of the district; whoever broke the law was beaten with them, rich and powerful men included. When the uncle of Jian Shuo, a Regular Palace Attendant, went abroad by night carrying a sword, Cao Cao caught him during his patrol and had him beaten with the cudgels. From then on, none within or beyond the court dared violate the law, and his formidable reputation spread far and wide. Later, he became magistrate of Dunqiu. When the Yellow Turbans rose in revolt, he was appointed Commandant of Cavalry and came to Yingchuan with five thousand horse and foot to aid the campaign. He arrived just as Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao were fleeing in defeat. Cao Cao barred their way and fell upon them, taking more than ten thousand heads and capturing countless banners, gongs, drums, and horses. Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao fought desperately and escaped. Cao Cao paid a visit to Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun, then immediately led his troops away in pursuit of Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao.

p.src: Meanwhile, Xuande led Guan Yu and Zhang Fei to Yingchuan. Hearing the din of battle and seeing flames light the heavens, he hastened forward with his troops, only to find the rebels already routed and scattered. Xuande met Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun and fully explained Lu Zhi's intentions. Huangfu Song said, “Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao are exhausted and at the end of their strength. They will surely flee to Guangzong and join Zhang Jue. You should go there this very night to lend your aid.” Xuande accepted the order and led his troops back the way they had come. Halfway there, he saw a cluster of soldiers escorting a prison cart. The prisoner inside was none other than Lu Zhi. Greatly shocked, Xuande swung down from his saddle and asked what had happened. Lu Zhi said, “I had Zhang Jue surrounded and was on the verge of defeating him. But because he employed sorcery, I could not win at once. The court sent the palace eunuch Zuo Feng to inspect the situation, and he demanded a bribe from me. I replied, ‘Even our provisions are in short supply. How could I have spare money with which to flatter an imperial envoy?’ Zuo Feng bore a grudge and, upon returning to court, accused me of hiding behind high ramparts and refusing battle, thereby sapping the army's spirit. The court was enraged and sent General of the Household Dong Zhuo to take command of my forces, while I was seized and sent back to the capital to answer charges.” When Zhang Fei heard this, he flew into a rage and wanted to kill the escorting soldiers and rescue Lu Zhi. Xuande hastily stopped him, saying, “The court will render a just judgment. How can you act so rashly?” The soldiers crowded around Lu Zhi and escorted him away.

p.src: Lord Guan said, “General Lu has been arrested. With another man commanding the army, we will have no one to rely upon if we go there. We had better return to Zhuo Commandery for now.” Xuande agreed and led the army north. Before two days had passed, a tremendous clamor suddenly rose from behind the hills. Xuande spurred with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei to the top of a high ridge and looked out. The imperial army was in utter rout, while behind it the hills and plains were packed with Yellow Turbans advancing like a flood; upon their banners were written in great characters, “General of Heaven.” Xuande said, “That is Zhang Jue! We must attack at once.” The three galloped forth at the head of their troops. Zhang Jue had just routed Dong Zhuo and was pressing the pursuit when the three warriors suddenly charged into him. His army fell into chaos and fled for more than fifty li. The three rescued Dong Zhuo and escorted him back to camp. Dong Zhuo asked what offices the three presently held. Xuande replied, “We hold no office.” Dong Zhuo treated them with great contempt and showed them no courtesy. After Xuande withdrew, Zhang Fei said furiously, “We risked our lives in bloody battle to save that wretch, and he treats us with such discourtesy! Unless I kill him, my anger will never be appeased!” He seized his sword and was about to enter the tent and kill Dong Zhuo. Indeed:
